references.text: The woman later testifies that Jesus told her everything she had done (John 4:29), which refers back to his revelation of her marital situation in verses 17–18.
Jesus shows the same supernatural knowledge of people when he sees Nathanael and knows him without having met him (John 1:47–48). This parallels his knowledge of the Samaritan woman's life.
John emphasizes that Jesus knew all people and knew what was in man (John 2:24–25). This omniscience is demonstrated in the conversation with the Samaritan woman.
The woman recognizes Jesus as a prophet precisely because he revealed the truth about her life (John 4:19). Her honest answer in verse 17 led to this recognition.
Jesus knew from the beginning who believed and who would betray him (John 6:64). This confirms the same pattern of divine omniscience shown in the conversation with the Samaritan woman.
Peter confesses: "Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you" (John 21:17). This affirms Jesus' omniscience, the same attribute he displays in his conversation with the Samaritan woman.

The five peoples who were settled in Samaria after the exile brought their own gods with them (2 Kings 17:29–33). Several interpreters see the woman's five husbands as a possible symbolic parallel to Samaria's five foreign worship practices.
